blocks.text: An Act To require the Attorney General to release all documents and records in possession of the Department of Justice relating to Jeffrey Epstein, and for other purposes.
Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled,
SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Epstein Files Transparency Act".
SEC. 2. RELEASE OF DOCUMENTS RELATING TO JEFFREY EPSTEIN.

(a) In General.--Not later than 30 days after the date of enactment of this Act, the Attorney General shall, subject to subsection (b), make publicly available in a searchable and downloadable format all unclassified records, documents, communications, and investigative materials in the possession of the Department of Justice, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation and United States Attorneys' Offices, that relate to:
(1) Jeffrey Epstein including all investigations, prosecutions, or custodial matters.
(2) Ghislaine Maxwell.

(3) Flight logs or travel records, including but not limited to manifests, itineraries, pilot records, and customs or immigration documentation, for any aircraft, vessel, or vehicle owned, operated, or used by Jeffrey Epstein or any related entity.
(4) Individuals, including government officials, named or referenced in connection with Epstein's criminal activities, civil settlements, immunity or plea agreements, or investigatory proceedings.
(5) Entities (corporate, nonprofit, academic, or governmental) with known or alleged ties to Epstein's trafficking or financial networks.
(6) Any immunity deals, non-prosecution agreements, plea bargains, or sealed settlements involving Epstein or his associates.
(7) Internal DOJ communications, including emails, memos, meeting notes, concerning decisions to charge, not charge, investigate, or decline to investigate Epstein or his associates.

(8) All communications, memoranda, directives, logs, or metadata concerning the destruction, deletion, alteration, misplacement, or concealment of documents, recordings, or electronic data related to Epstein, his associates, his detention and death, or any investigative files.

(9) Documentation of Epstein's detention or death, including incident reports, witness interviews, medical examiner files, autopsy reports, and written records detailing the circumstances and cause of death.
(b) Prohibited Grounds for Withholding.--

(1) No record shall be withheld, delayed, or redacted on the basis of embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity, including to any government official, public figure, or foreign dignitary.
(c) Permitted Withholdings.--
(1) The Attorney general may withhold or redact the segregable portions of records that--

(A) contain personally identifiable information of victims or victims' personal and medical files and similar files the disclosure of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy;
(B) depict or contain child sexual abuse materials (CSAM) as defined under 18 U.S.C. 2256 and prohibited under 18 U.S.C. 2252-2252A;
(C) would jeopardize an active federal investigation or ongoing prosecution, provided that such withholding is narrowly tailored and temporary;
(D) depict or contain images of death, physical abuse, or injury of any person; or

(E) contain information specifically authorized under criteria established by an Executive order to be kept secret in the interest of national defense or foreign policy and are in fact properly classified pursuant to such Executive order.
(2) All redactions must be accompanied by a written justification published in the Federal Register and submitted to Congress.

(3) To the extent that any covered information would otherwise be redacted or withheld as classified information under this section, the Attorney General shall declassify that classified information to the maximum extent possible.

(A) If the Attorney General makes a determination that covered information may not be declassified and made available in a manner that protects the national security of the United States, including methods or sources related to national security, the Attorney General shall release an unclassified summary for each of the redacted or withheld classified information.

(4) All decisions to classify any covered information after July 1, 2025 shall be published in the Federal Register and submitted to Congress, including the date of classification, the identity of the classifying authority, and an unclassified summary of the justification.
SEC. 3. REPORT TO CONGRESS.
Within 15 days of completion of the release required under Section 2, the Attorney General shall submit to the House and Senate Committees on the Judiciary a report listing:
(1) All categories of records released and withheld.
(2) A summary of redactions made, including legal basis.
(3) A list of all government officials and politically exposed persons named or referenced in the released materials, with no redactions permitted under subsection (b)(1).

cls.function: A freestanding mandate on one official, the Attorney General
cls.banner: The Epstein Files Transparency Act is binding law. It orders the Attorney General to publish Justice Department records about Jeffrey Epstein within 30 days.
cls.checks: This analysis ran every family of checks on the Epstein Files Transparency Act. For a freestanding mandate on one official, the checks on definitions, enforcement and the scope of who is bound come first.

stated.t: To require the Attorney General to release all documents and records in possession of the Department of Justice relating to Jeffrey Epstein, and for other purposes.

marketed.t: Records cannot be held back on the basis of embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity.
marketed.l: CP24 summary of the bill text

marketed.t: The Attorney General told reporters the Department would follow the law with maximum transparency while protecting victims.

ladder.mechanism: The Epstein Files Transparency Act orders one official, the Attorney General, to publish one department's unclassified records about Jeffrey Epstein within 30 days.
ladder.outcome: The intended outcome is that the public can read the government's records on Jeffrey Epstein and the people connected to him.
ladder.aim: The broader aim is accountability for those involved with Epstein and for the government's own handling of the case, without further harm to survivors.

promises.p: The Act's long title states that it requires the Attorney General to release all documents and records in possession of the Department of Justice relating to Jeffrey Epstein.
promises.why: The operative text in section 2(a) reaches only unclassified Epstein records in the possession of the Department of Justice. Epstein records held by other agencies, and classified records, are outside the mandate.

promises.p: Section 2(a) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act promises that the Justice Department's Epstein records will be released within 30 days.
promises.why: Section 2(a) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act states the 30-day deadline, but the Act attaches no consequence to missing it and contains no enforcement clause of its own. The deadline passed with about half the pages of Epstein records unreleased.

promises.p: Section 2(b)(1) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act promises that no Epstein record will be withheld, delayed or redacted on the basis of embarrassment, reputational harm or political sensitivity.
promises.why: The prohibition in section 2(b)(1) is clear, but the five permitted grounds for withholding in subsection (c) are judged by the same official, the Attorney General, and the Act builds in no outside review. A court began reviewing withheld Epstein documents only in July 2026, in a suit brought under a different statute.

promises.p: The Attorney General said the Department of Justice would protect victims while releasing the Epstein records.
promises.why: Section 2(c)(1)(A) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act permits, but does not require, redaction of victims' identifying information from the Epstein records.

promises.p: Section 3(3) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act promises a list of the government officials and politically exposed persons named in the Epstein files.
promises.why: The list under section 3(3) is due only after the release is complete, goes to two congressional committees and not to the public, and uses a term, "politically exposed persons", that the Epstein Files Transparency Act does not define.

questions.q: Section 2(a) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act says the Attorney General "shall" publish the Epstein records. Where does the Act switch to "may", and what does each "may" leave to the Attorney General's choice?
questions.a: Most of that discretion appears in one place: section 2(c)(1), under which the Attorney General "may withhold or redact" five categories of material in the Epstein records. The first category is victims' identifying information. Release of the records is commanded, and protection of victims is optional.

questions.q: Which words in section 2(a) narrow the promise of "all documents and records" about Jeffrey Epstein, and which Epstein records does each word leave out?
questions.a: Two limiting phrases in section 2(a) do the narrowing. "Unclassified" excludes any Epstein record the executive branch has classified, and the executive branch controls classification. "In the possession of the Department of Justice" excludes Epstein records held anywhere else.

questions.q: Which parts of the federal government other than the Justice Department would hold records about Jeffrey Epstein?
questions.a: A financier with international travel, a federal prosecution and a death in federal custody leaves records well beyond one department. Those holders include the Treasury Department and its financial crimes bureau, the IRS, customs and immigration agencies, the State Department, intelligence agencies, the Bureau of Prisons (a component of the Justice Department) and the National Archives. The Act names only the Justice Department.

s.l: Draft Title VII, listing additional sources

questions.q: If the Attorney General publishes no Epstein records by the 30-day deadline in section 2(a), what happens next, and who can make it happen?
questions.a: The Epstein Files Transparency Act provides no remedy. Its sponsors asked one court to appoint a monitor and were told the Act gives that court no such authority. A journalist later obtained an injunction under the Administrative Procedure Act, more than six months after the deadline.

s.l: United States v. Maxwell, opinion of January 21, 2026
Account of the June 2026 injunction

questions.q: Who is affected if the Epstein Files Transparency Act works exactly as written, including the people it is meant to protect?
questions.a: The survivors are the people affected. A statute that mandates publication of the Epstein records at speed and makes redaction of survivors' information optional exposes them to the errors of a rushed review. Survivors and their lawyers reported names appearing in released files and asked the Justice Department's inspector general to step in.

s.l: Survivors on failure to redact victim identities
Survivors urge DOJ watchdog review

questions.q: For an Attorney General who preferred to release fewer Epstein records, what is the least costly lawful path under the Act?
questions.a: The text of the Act leaves three such paths open. The Attorney General can classify records or keep them classified, can open or point to an active investigation, since the Act lets that official decide what would "jeopardize" one, or can use the broad category for images of death, abuse or injury "of any person".

s.l: How one major exception could allow withholding

questions.q: How did the closest earlier federal records law handle the same problems that the Epstein Files Transparency Act faces?
questions.a: The 1992 law on Kennedy assassination records reached records across the federal government and created an independent review board to decide postponements of release. The Epstein Files Transparency Act has neither feature.

s.l: National Archives: JFK Assassination Records background

questions.q: Do the internal cross-references in the Epstein Files Transparency Act point to the parts of the Act they need to?
questions.a: Two cross-references in the Epstein Files Transparency Act do not. Section 2(a) is made "subject to subsection (b)", which lists the prohibited grounds for withholding, and never mentions subsection (c), which lists the permitted withholdings. Section 3(3) cites "subsection (b)(1)" although section 3 has no subsections.

questions.q: What event starts the 15-day period for the Attorney General's report to Congress under section 3?
questions.a: Section 3 of the Epstein Files Transparency Act runs the period from "completion of the release". If the Justice Department never declares the release complete, the report never comes due.

questions.q: What is the smallest set of amendments to the Epstein Files Transparency Act that would deliver its stated purpose?
questions.a: Four changes would do so: make redaction of victims' information mandatory in its own paragraph, extend the mandate to every agency holding responsive Epstein records, have someone other than the official making withholding decisions review them, and attach a consequence to the deadline.

a.ctx: The Attorney general may withhold or redact

findings.title: Section 2(c)(1)(A) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act permits, but does not require, the Attorney General to redact victims' identifying information from released Epstein records.
findings.plain: The Epstein Files Transparency Act orders the Epstein records released but only permits, and does not require, the Attorney General to redact victims' names and personal details. A single word, "may", makes the difference between a duty and a discretion.
findings.tech: Section 2(a) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act uses "shall" for publication of the Epstein records. Section 2(c)(1) uses "may" for all five withholding categories, including subparagraph (A), victims' personally identifiable information. The Justice Department read the Act the same way, telling a federal court the Act "does not require withholding or redacting of victim information".
findings.use: Under a 30-day mandate, the Attorney General can publish the Epstein records first and redact victims' information imperfectly, and a survivor whose information is released has no statutory duty to point to.

s.l: Department of Justice letter, S.D.N.Y.
Survivors on failure to redact

am.label: Minimal fix: change "may" to "shall"
am.instr: Section 2(c)(1) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act (Public Law 119-38) is amended by striking "may" and inserting "shall".

ops.ctx: The Attorney general may withhold or redact
ops.w: shall

am.cost: Testing this amendment against the Epstein Files Transparency Act shows a side effect. The same "may" in section 2(c)(1) governs all five categories, so changing that one word would also require withholding of everything relating to an active investigation, images of injury and classified material. The amendment would protect victims and mandate more secrecy at the same time.

am.label: Targeted fix: a separate, mandatory protection for victims
am.instr: Section 2(c) is amended (1) in paragraph (1), by striking subparagraph (A) and redesignating subparagraphs (B) through (E) as subparagraphs (A) through (D); and (2) by inserting before paragraph (1) a new paragraph requiring redaction of victim information.

ops.before: The Attorney general may withhold or redact
ops.w: (1) REQUIRED REDACTION.--The Attorney General shall redact from any record made publicly available under subsection (a) the personally identifiable information of any victim, and shall withhold victims' personal and medical files and similar files the disclosure of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy, unless the victim consents in writing to disclosure.

ops.q: (A) contain personally identifiable information of victims or victims' personal and medical files and similar files the disclosure of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy;

am.cost: Mandatory redaction would slow the release of Epstein records and require staff. It would also require a definition of "victim", which the Act lacks. The amendment's consent clause would allow survivors who want to be named to be named.

findings.title: Section 2(a) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act covers only Epstein records in the possession of the Department of Justice, not records held by other federal agencies.
findings.plain: The Epstein Files Transparency Act reaches Epstein records held by the Department of Justice, and the only offices it names, the FBI and the United States Attorneys' Offices, are components of that Department. Records about the same people held elsewhere in the federal government are not covered.
findings.tech: Section 2(a) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act limits the mandate to records "in the possession of the Department of Justice, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation and United States Attorneys' Offices". The "including" clause lists components of the Justice Department and does not extend the mandate to other agencies. An Epstein record transferred out of the Department, or never held by it, is outside the Act.
findings.use: Under section 2(a), the location of an Epstein record determines whether it is published. Material at the Treasury Department, the Department of Homeland Security, the State Department or an intelligence agency is not reached, and material the Justice Department passes to another agency leaves the Act's reach.

s.l: National Archives: the 1992 JFK records law reached records government-wide

am.label: Extend the mandate to every federal agency
am.instr: Section 2(a) is amended by striking "in the possession of the Department of Justice, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation and United States Attorneys' Offices," and inserting "in the possession, custody, or control of any Federal agency (as defined in section 551 of title 5, United States Code), including the Department of Justice, the Department of the Treasury, the Department of State, the Department of Homeland Security, each element of the intelligence community, and the National Archives and Records Administration,".

ops.q: in the possession of the Department of Justice, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation and United States Attorneys' Offices,
ops.w: in the possession, custody, or control of any Federal agency (as defined in section 551 of title 5, United States Code), including the Department of Justice, the Department of the Treasury, the Department of State, the Department of Homeland Security, each element of the intelligence community, and the National Archives and Records Administration,

am.cost: The Attorney General cannot compel other agency heads, so each agency head would need to be made responsible for that agency's Epstein records. Some record types, such as tax returns and suspicious activity reports, are protected by other statutes that the amendment would need to address by name.

findings.pat: Limiter word controlled by the regulated party
findings.title: Section 2(a) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act requires release only of unclassified Epstein records, and the executive branch, including the Justice Department, decides what is classified.
findings.plain: Section 2(a) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act requires release only of unclassified Epstein records. The executive branch decides what is classified, so the Attorney General, who is ordered to release the records, also has a say over what counts as releasable.
findings.tech: Section 2(a) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act covers "all unclassified records". Section 2(c)(3) softens this limit by directing declassification "to the maximum extent possible" and unclassified summaries otherwise, and section 2(c)(4) requires notice of classification decisions made after July 1, 2025. However, "maximum extent possible" is a feasibility qualifier judged by the same official, the Attorney General, and notice of a new classification does not undo it.
findings.use: The executive branch can classify Epstein material, or leave it classified, and replace it with a summary written by the agency withholding it.

s.l: Draft Title VII on congressional declassification

am.label: Classified annex to Congress and independent review
am.instr: Section 2(c)(3) is amended by adding at the end the following: "(B) Not later than 30 days after making a determination under subparagraph (A), the Attorney General shall transmit the unredacted covered information to the Select Committee on Intelligence of the Senate and the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence of the House of Representatives, and shall refer the determination to the Public Interest Declassification Board for review."

ops.after: the Attorney General shall release an unclassified summary
ops.w: (B) Not later than 30 days after making a determination under subparagraph (A), the Attorney General shall transmit the unredacted covered information to the Select Committee on Intelligence of the Senate and the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence of the House of Representatives, and shall refer the determination to the Public Interest Declassification Board for review.

am.cost: The amendment adds oversight of classified Epstein records but not public release. A stronger version, in which Congress itself orders declassification, would raise a separation of powers dispute and would be litigated.

two.dec: Should executive branch decisions to classify Epstein records be subject to review by a court or an independent body?

views.why: Intelligence agencies regard classification, including of any Epstein records they hold, as the way sources and methods are protected.

s.l: Rep. Mace letter to the CIA

a.q: Not later than 30 days after the date of enactment of this Act

findings.title: Section 2(a) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act gives the Attorney General 30 days to release the Epstein records and specifies no consequence for missing that deadline.
findings.plain: Section 2(a) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act sets a 30-day deadline for release of the Epstein records but says nothing about what follows if the Attorney General misses it. The Act gives no one the power to enforce the deadline.
findings.tech: The 30-day deadline in section 2(a) is not paired with a penalty, a default rule, a reporting trigger or a cause of action anywhere in the Epstein Files Transparency Act. Courts are generally reluctant to compel agency action on a statutory timetable without a clear enforcement provision.
findings.use: The Justice Department can release the Epstein records in batches on its own schedule.

s.l: DOJ missing deadline to publish all files

findings.pat: Cross-reference points to the wrong provision
findings.title: Section 2(a) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act makes release of Epstein records subject to the prohibited grounds in subsection (b), not the permitted withholdings in subsection (c).
findings.plain: The release requirement in section 2(a) is stated to be "subject to subsection (b)". Subsection (b) lists reasons that cannot be used to withhold Epstein records. The reasons that can be used are in subsection (c), which section 2(a) never mentions.
findings.tech: As enacted, section 2(a) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act is "subject to subsection (b)", the prohibited grounds. The permitted withholdings are in section 2(c). A Senate companion text made the release duty subject to its permitted-withholdings subsection, which suggests the reference was not updated when the subsections were reordered. Read literally, the relationship between the "shall" in subsection (a) and the "may" in subsection (c) is left to inference.
findings.use: Either side in a dispute over withheld Epstein records can argue from the mismatched reference: that subsection (c) does not qualify subsection (a) at all, or that subsection (c) is a free-standing discretion not bounded by subsection (a).

s.l: Senate companion text, S. 2557

am.label: Correct the cross-reference in section 2(a)
am.instr: Section 2(a) is amended by striking "subject to subsection (b)" and inserting "subject to subsections (b) and (c)".

ops.w: subject to subsections (b) and (c)

am.cost: The amendment, which makes the release of Epstein records subject to both subsections (b) and (c), carries no cost beyond confirming the intended reading.

findings.title: Section 3(3) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act, on the Attorney General's report to Congress, cites "subsection (b)(1)", but section 3 has no subsections.
findings.plain: Section 3 of the Epstein Files Transparency Act, on the Attorney General's report to Congress about the Epstein records, points to "subsection (b)(1)", but section 3 has no subsections. The reference almost certainly means section 2(b)(1).
findings.tech: Under ordinary drafting convention, an unqualified "subsection (b)(1)" refers to the section in which it appears, and section 3 of the Epstein Files Transparency Act has paragraphs (1) through (3) only. The phrase "no redactions permitted under subsection (b)(1)" is also ambiguous, because section 2(b)(1) prohibits grounds for withholding and does not permit redactions.
findings.use: It is unclear whether the Attorney General may redact names in the section 3(3) list delivered to Congress on the grounds in section 2(c).

am.label: Correct the reference and clarify its meaning
am.instr: Section 3(3) is amended by striking "with no redactions permitted under subsection (b)(1)" and inserting "with no name withheld or redacted on any ground described in section 2(b)(1)".

ops.q: with no redactions permitted under subsection (b)(1)
ops.w: with no name withheld or redacted on any ground described in section 2(b)(1)

am.cost: This amendment to section 3(3) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act has no identified cost.

findings.title: Section 3(3) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act requires a list of "politically exposed persons" named in the Epstein records and does not define that phrase.
findings.plain: The report to Congress under section 3 must list "politically exposed persons" named in the Epstein files. The Act does not say who qualifies.
findings.tech: The phrase "politically exposed persons" comes from anti-money-laundering practice, where it generally refers to senior foreign officials and their close associates. Without a definition or a cross-reference in the Epstein Files Transparency Act, the official who compiles the list, the Attorney General, chooses its breadth.
findings.use: A narrow reading of "politically exposed persons" by the Attorney General shortens the list of names from the Epstein records delivered to Congress.

findings.pat: Exception controlled by the regulated party
findings.title: Section 2(c)(1)(C) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act lets the Attorney General withhold Epstein records for an active investigation with no stated standard, time limit or external review.
findings.plain: Section 2(c)(1)(C) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act permits withholding of Epstein records whose release would jeopardize an active investigation, provided the withholding is "narrowly tailored and temporary". The Act does not say how narrow, how long, or who reviews the decision.
findings.tech: Section 2(c)(1)(C) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act conditions the exception for active investigations on tailoring and temporariness but supplies no time limit, no periodic re-justification and no reviewer. The Justice Department, which decides whether an investigation is active, is the same department applying the exception.
findings.use: An open investigation can support withholding of Epstein records for as long as the investigation stays open.

s.l: How one major exception could allow withholding

am.label: Add a 180-day limit and a renewal requirement
am.instr: Section 2(c)(1)(C) is amended by striking "narrowly tailored and temporary" and inserting "narrowly tailored, expires not later than 180 days after it begins unless the Attorney General certifies in writing to the Committees on the Judiciary of the House of Representatives and the Senate the specific investigation or prosecution that continued withholding would jeopardize, and is renewed only by a new certification every 180 days".

ops.w: narrowly tailored, expires not later than 180 days after it begins unless the Attorney General certifies in writing to the Committees on the Judiciary of the House of Representatives and the Senate the specific investigation or prosecution that continued withholding would jeopardize, and is renewed only by a new certification every 180 days

am.cost: The Attorney General's certifications to Congress for continued withholding of Epstein records can become routine. The 180-day figure is a policy choice.

a.q: depict or contain images of death, physical abuse, or injury of any person

findings.title: Section 2(c)(1)(D) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act lets the Attorney General withhold any Epstein record that contains an image of death, abuse or injury of any person.
findings.plain: Section 2(c)(1)(D) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act permits withholding or redaction of any Epstein record that depicts or contains images of death, abuse or injury "of any person". The category protects dignity, and it also reaches a large amount of evidence.
findings.tech: Section 2(c)(1)(D) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act is not limited to victims or to images whose release would be an invasion of privacy. Because section 2(c)(1) speaks of "segregable portions", the better reading confines withholding to the images themselves, but the word "contain" invites withholding of the surrounding record.
findings.use: The Justice Department can treat reports in the Epstein records that include a photograph as records it may withhold in full.

a.q: Within 15 days of completion of the release

findings.title: Section 3 of the Epstein Files Transparency Act makes the Attorney General's report to Congress due 15 days after the release is complete, and no one must certify completion.
findings.plain: Section 3 of the Epstein Files Transparency Act requires the Attorney General to report to Congress within 15 days of completing the release of Epstein records. If the release is never declared complete, the report never comes due.
findings.tech: Section 3 of the Epstein Files Transparency Act ties the reporting duty to "completion of the release required under Section 2" and not to the 30-day deadline. A rolling release has no completion date unless the Justice Department announces one. The report also goes to two committees, with no requirement that it be public.
findings.use: The list of withheld categories of Epstein records, the legal basis for redactions and the list of named officials can be deferred indefinitely.

findings.pat: No enforcement mechanism in the statute
findings.title: The Epstein Files Transparency Act contains no penalty, no judicial review provision and no private right of action to enforce its release requirements.
findings.plain: The Epstein Files Transparency Act contains no penalty, no provision for judicial review and no express right of action. When the deadline passed, one court turned away the Act's own sponsors. A different court later allowed a journalist's suit under a general statute, more than six months after the deadline.
findings.tech: The Epstein Files Transparency Act contains no cause of action, no grant of jurisdiction, no role for an inspector general and no consequence for noncompliance. Enforcement has depended on finding a general statute that fits and a plaintiff with standing. A bill introduced later, H.R. 9694, would add enforcement by state attorneys general and by victims.

(b) The court shall examine withheld or redacted material in camera and shall determine de novo whether each withholding is authorized by section 2(c). SEC. 4. ENFORCEMENT.

findings.title: The Epstein Files Transparency Act assigns release and withholding decisions to the Attorney General, and both Attorneys General since enactment previously served as lawyers for President Trump.
findings.plain: Sections 2 and 3 of the Epstein Files Transparency Act give the Attorney General the duty to release the Epstein records, the discretion to withhold them and the duty to report on what was withheld. Both people who have held that office since enactment previously served as lawyers for President Trump: Pam Bondi until April 2026, and Todd Blanche since then. News reports state that Pam Bondi told the President in May 2025 that his name appeared in the Epstein files, at a briefing that Todd Blanche attended. The Act has no recusal rule and names no other decision-maker.
findings.tech: The President appoints the Attorney General and may remove that official, and he removed Pam Bondi in April 2026. The reports of the May 2025 briefing say the significance of the references to the President is not clear, and the Department of Justice said that nothing in the files warranted further investigation. A separate, structural conflict exists whoever holds the office, because section 2(a) of the Act covers the Department's own internal communications about decisions to charge or not charge Epstein. Congress has addressed comparable conflicts before, through the independent counsel provisions of the Ethics in Government Act of 1978, which lapsed in 1999, and through the independent review board in the 1992 Kennedy records law.
findings.use: An Attorney General who previously represented the President can apply the withholding categories in section 2(c) of the Act to Epstein records that concern the President, and no independent body is positioned to test those decisions.

findings.title: The Epstein Files Transparency Act does not define "victim", "associate" or "related entity", although those words decide whose information is protected and which records are released.
findings.plain: The Epstein Files Transparency Act contains no definitions. It does not specify who is a "victim", who counts as one of Epstein's "associates", or what a "related entity" is.
findings.tech: The word "victims" controls the reach of the privacy protection in section 2(c)(1)(A) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act. The word "associates" controls the scope of categories (6), (7) and (8) in section 2(a). Neither is defined or cross-referenced to an existing statutory definition.
findings.use: A narrow reading of "victim" exposes people who were never formally identified as victims in a charging document. A narrow reading of "associates" shrinks the release of Epstein records.

am.label: Add a definition of "victim"

In this Act, the term 'victim' means any individual who was, or who is described in a covered record as having been, subjected to sexual abuse, trafficking, or exploitation by Jeffrey Epstein or any associate of Jeffrey Epstein, whether or not the individual was identified in any charging document, and includes any individual who was a minor at the time of the events described."

cls.function: A direct order to one official, the Attorney General
cls.banner: The Epstein Files Transparency Act is a law, and it must be obeyed. It tells the Attorney General to publish Justice Department records on Jeffrey Epstein. The deadline is 30 days.
cls.checks: This review used every kind of check on the Epstein Files Transparency Act. The law gives one official a direct order. So the review looked first at what its words mean, how it is enforced, and who must obey it.

stated.t: To require the Attorney General to release all documents and records in possession of the Department of Justice relating to Jeffrey Epstein, and for other purposes.

marketed.t: Records cannot be held back on the basis of embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity.

ladder.mechanism: The Epstein files law gives an order to one official, the Attorney General. That official must publish records about Jeffrey Epstein within 30 days. The law covers only one department's records that are not marked secret.
ladder.outcome: The goal is that the public can read what the government has on Jeffrey Epstein. That includes records on the people tied to him.
ladder.aim: The larger aim is that the people involved with Epstein must answer for what they did. So must the government that handled his case. The law aims to do this without more harm to survivors.

promises.p: The Epstein files law has a long title. It says the Attorney General must release all of the Justice Department's documents and records on Jeffrey Epstein.
promises.why: But the main order in the Epstein files law covers less. It covers only Epstein records that the Justice Department holds and that are not marked secret. Records at other agencies, and records marked secret, are left out.

promises.p: The Epstein files law promised that the Justice Department's Epstein records would all be out in 30 days.
promises.why: The Epstein files law sets a 30-day deadline. But it says nothing about what happens if the deadline is missed. It gives no one the power to enforce it. The deadline passed with about half the pages of Epstein records still not out.

promises.p: The Epstein files law made a promise. No Epstein record would be held back, delayed or blacked out because it is embarrassing. The same goes for harm to someone's reputation, or because a record is politically touchy.
promises.why: The ban on those reasons is clear. But the Epstein files law also lists five reasons that can be used to hold records back. The Attorney General judges those reasons, and no one outside checks. A court began to look at held-back Epstein papers only in July 2026. That case was brought under a different law.

promises.p: The Attorney General made a promise about the Epstein files. The Justice Department would keep victims safe as it put them out.
promises.why: The Epstein files law lets the Attorney General hide the names and details of victims in the Epstein records. It does not make the Attorney General do it.

promises.p: The Epstein files law made a promise. It said there would be a list of names in the files. The list would include government officials and "politically exposed persons".
promises.why: The list is due only after the Justice Department finishes putting out the Epstein records. It goes to two committees of Congress, not to the public. And the law never says who counts as one of the "politically exposed persons".

questions.q: The Epstein files law says the Attorney General "shall" publish the records, which means must. Where does the law switch to "may", and what does each "may" let the Attorney General choose?
questions.a: Most of the choice is in one part of the Epstein files law. It says the Attorney General "may" hold back or black out five kinds of material. The first kind is facts that show who the victims are. So the records must come out, but protecting victims is up to the Attorney General.

questions.q: Which words in the Epstein files law shrink its promise of "all documents and records", and what do they leave out?
questions.a: Two limits do the shrinking. The Epstein files law covers only records that are not marked secret. Officials who work under the President decide what is marked secret. The law also covers only records the Justice Department holds. Records kept anywhere else are left out.

questions.q: Epstein records may be kept outside the Justice Department. Which other parts of the federal government would have them?
questions.a: Epstein was a financier, a man who dealt in large sums of money. He traveled to other countries. Federal prosecutors charged him, and he died in federal custody. A man like that leaves records in many places. They include the Treasury Department and its office for money crimes, the IRS, and the customs and immigration agencies. They also include the State Department, spy agencies and the National Archives. So does the Bureau of Prisons, which is part of the Justice Department. The Epstein files law names only the Justice Department.

questions.q: Say an Attorney General wanted to put out fewer Epstein records. What is the easiest legal way to do it under this law?
questions.a: The wording of the Epstein files law leaves three ways open. The Attorney General can mark records secret or keep them secret. Or the Attorney General can start an investigation or point to one. The law lets that same official decide what would "jeopardize" one, meaning put it at risk. questions.a: The 1992 law on Kennedy assassination records covered records across the whole federal government. It also set up an independent review board to decide when a release could be put off. The Epstein files law has neither of these.

questions.q: When the Epstein files law points to its own parts, does it point to the right ones?
questions.a: Two pointers in the Epstein files law go to the wrong place. The order to release says it is limited by the part that bans some reasons for holding records back. It never names the part that lists the reasons that are allowed. And the part on the report to Congress points to a smaller part of itself that does not exist.

questions.q: What starts the 15-day deadline for the Attorney General's report to Congress on the Epstein records?
questions.a: The 15 days start at the "completion of the release", meaning when all the Epstein records are out. If the Justice Department never says the release is done, the report is never due.

questions.q: What is the smallest set of changes to the Epstein files law that would do what it set out to do?
questions.a: Four changes to the Epstein files law would do it. First, a separate rule would require hiding victims' details. Second, the order would cover every agency that holds Epstein records. Third, someone other than the Attorney General would check choices to hold records back. Fourth, missing the deadline would have a consequence.

findings.title: The law lets the government hide victims' names in the Epstein files. It does not make the government do it.
findings.plain: The law tells the Attorney General, the country's top law enforcement official, to publish the Epstein files. It says the Attorney General "may" hide victims' names and personal details. "May" means allowed, not required. So hiding the names is a choice.
findings.tech: The Epstein files law uses "shall", meaning must, for putting out the records. It uses "may" for all five kinds of material the Attorney General can hold back. findings.pat: The regulated official is the only decision-maker
findings.title: The Attorney General decides which Epstein records to hold back. No one outside the Justice Department checks those choices.
findings.plain: The Attorney General decides which Epstein records to hold back, writes the reasons and reports on them. No one outside the Justice Department checks those choices.
findings.tech: A 1992 law on Kennedy assassination records set up an independent review board. It decided when a release could be put off. The Epstein files law has no such board. Its ban on holding records back to avoid embarrassment depends on the good faith of the official who might be embarrassed.
findings.use: An Epstein record held back for a banned reason, like shame, could be given an allowed reason instead.

bigger.issue: Government openness and accountability in the Jeffrey Epstein case
bigger.lead: Say the Epstein files law worked just as written. It would only deliver the Justice Department's records that are not marked secret. The public's questions about the Epstein case go further than that.

map.part: Justice Department investigation and prosecution files on Epstein
map.note: The Epstein files law covers these files. They are the main thing it orders released.

map.part: Financial, tax, immigration, spy agency and archive records held by other agencies
map.note: The Epstein files law reaches only records the Justice Department holds. So it does not cover these records.
The Epstein files law tells the Attorney General to lift secret markings "to the maximum extent possible". That means as far as can be done. If not, the Attorney General must put out summaries.
The Epstein files law lets the Attorney General hide victims' names and details. But it does not make the Attorney General do it.

map.part: Records sealed by courts and grand jury material
map.note: The Epstein files law says nothing about court orders that seal records or the secrecy rules for grand juries. The Justice Department asked courts for permission on its own.

s.l: DOJ letter, S.D.N.Y.

map.part: Outside review of held-back Epstein records
map.note: The Epstein files law sets up no outside review. A court began to look at held-back documents in July 2026, in a lawsuit under a different law. The Government Accountability Office, which checks government work for Congress, is looking at the hidden parts.

map.part: Consequences for anyone the Epstein records point to
map.note: The Epstein files law only requires records to be released. It does not require anyone to investigate, refer cases or bring charges.

map.part: Records held by Epstein's estate, banks and other private parties
map.note: The Epstein files law covers only government records, so private records like these are left out.

stake.want: Survivors and their lawyers want the Epstein records out without showing who the survivors are. The Justice Department took down several thousand files it had put out. They may have shown who victims were.

stake.role: Journalists and advocates for open government
stake.want: Journalists and open-government groups want as many Epstein records out as possible. They want the names of powerful people left showing. They want a reason given for all that is held back.

stake.role: The Justice Department
stake.want: The Justice Department has said it will hide victim details as fully as the Epstein files law allows.

stake.role: People named in the Epstein files but not accused of crimes
stake.want: Some people are named in the Epstein files but not accused. They do not want to be tied in public to crimes they were not charged with.

stake.role: Prosecutors with open cases
stake.want: Prosecutors with open cases do not want any Epstein records to come out that could harm a case still going on.

stake.role: Intelligence agencies such as the CIA
stake.want: Spy agencies do not want a law that forces out their files. Such a law could be used as an example later. The CIA will not say whether or not it holds Epstein records.

stake.role: A judge who reads laws by their exact words
stake.want: A judge who reads laws by their exact words applies the Epstein files law as written. That judge will not fill in what Congress left out.

stake.role: A judge who reads laws by their purpose
stake.want: A judge who reads laws by their purpose settles doubts in favor of what the Epstein files law was trying to do.

stake.role: A legislative drafter
stake.want: A person who writes bills wants every key word in the Epstein files law defined. That person also wants every pointer checked and every link to other laws spelled out.

conflicts.who: Todd Blanche, Attorney General since April 2026
conflicts.claim: Attorney General Todd Blanche now decides which Epstein records stay held back. He used to be President Trump's personal lawyer.
conflicts.detail: Todd Blanche was Deputy Attorney General, the second-highest Justice Department official, when the Epstein files law took effect. He stepped in as acting Attorney General in April 2026. The Senate confirmed him by a vote of 50 to 49 in August 2026. News reports describe him as the President's former personal lawyer and close ally. News reports also say he was at a briefing in May 2025. At that briefing, the President was told his name appeared in the Epstein files. Those reports say it is not clear how significant the references are. The law has no rule telling an official with a tie like this to step aside.

s.l: The Week, August 10, 2026
Star Tribune (New York Times report), July 2025

conflicts.who: Pam Bondi, Attorney General until April 2026
conflicts.claim: Pam Bondi was Attorney General when the first Epstein files came out. She had been a lawyer for President Trump.
conflicts.detail: Pam Bondi joined President Trump's legal team during his first impeachment trial in 2020. News reports say she told the President in May 2025 that his name was in the Epstein files. The reports also say she and her deputy said nothing in the files called for further investigation or prosecution. The President removed her as Attorney General in April 2026.

s.l: Fortune, November 22, 2024
Star Tribune (New York Times report), July 2025
The Week, August 10, 2026

conflicts.claim: News reports say the Epstein files name President Trump. He can pick or remove the Attorney General at any time.
conflicts.detail: The Epstein files law lets the Attorney General alone decide what to put out and what to hold back. The President removed one Attorney General in April 2026. He picked her replacement. The law has no separate process for Epstein records about the President.

s.l: Star Tribune (New York Times report), July 2025
The Week, August 10, 2026

conflicts.claim: The Justice Department decides what to release from records of its own choices in the Epstein case.
conflicts.detail: The Epstein records include the Justice Department's internal messages about whether to charge Epstein. They also include its deals not to prosecute him and records of his death in federal custody. The law names no one outside the Justice Department to decide what is released. It requires no outside check on what is held back.
